concepts.title: Counting Iterations of the range Function

questions.q: How many numbers does range(2, 10) generate, and which ones? Use the method 'Counting Iterations of the range Function'. Work with: start = 3, step = 20, stop = 60. Carry the chain through step by step and give the final value of items.

How many iterations does the loop 'for i in range(20, 30, 2)' make? Use the method 'Counting Iterations of the range Function'. Work with: start = 150, step = 18, stop = 300. Carry the chain through step by step and give the final value of items.
Explain in your own words what 'Counting Iterations of the range Function' refers to.
questions.a: The range(start, stop, step) function generates integers from start up to but excluding stop, moving by step; the number of values it yields equals the span divided by the step, rounded upward, and a negative step walks downwards.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Counting Iterations of the range Function'.
questions.a: The stop value itself never appears in the generated sequence, and omitting start or step defaults them to 0 and 1.

questions.q: Write the standard relation used for 'Counting Iterations of the range Function', in plain ASCII form.
Using the method 'Positive Difference with Selection', work with: first = 12, second = 120. Carry the chain through step by step and give the final value of positive_diff.
Take the relation taught for 'Positive Difference with Selection' and work with: first = 25, second = 300. Carry the chain through step by step and give the final value of positive_diff.
Explain in your own words what 'Positive Difference with Selection' refers to.
questions.a: An if..else statement picks between two paths, so subtracting the smaller number from the larger always yields a positive difference; equivalently, taking the square root of the squared difference removes the sign.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Positive Difference with Selection'.
questions.a: Whichever branch runs, the same subtraction pair is ordered so the result never goes negative.

questions.q: Write the standard relation used for 'Positive Difference with Selection', in plain ASCII form.

concepts.title: Sum of Digits of an Integer

questions.q: Using the method 'Sum of Digits of an Integer', work with: number = 256. Carry the chain through step by step and give the final value of digit_sum.
Take the relation taught for 'Sum of Digits of an Integer' and work with: number = 512. Carry the chain through step by step and give the final value of digit_sum.
Explain in your own words what 'Sum of Digits of an Integer' refers to.
questions.a: A while loop can peel one digit per pass: the remainder on division by 10 is the last digit, floor division by 10 discards it, and the loop adds each peeled digit into a running total until nothing remains.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Sum of Digits of an Integer'.
questions.a: Modulus 10 captures the current last digit and floor division by 10 shortens the number for the next pass.

questions.q: Write the standard relation used for 'Sum of Digits of an Integer', in plain ASCII form.

concepts.title: Factorial of a Number with a Loop

questions.q: Using the method 'Factorial of a Number with a Loop', work with: num = 75. Carry the chain through step by step and give the final value of fact5.
Take the relation taught for 'Factorial of a Number with a Loop' and work with: num = 5. Carry the chain through step by step and give the final value of fact5.
Explain in your own words what 'Factorial of a Number with a Loop' refers to.
questions.a: The factorial of n multiplies every whole number from 1 up to n; a for loop with range(1, num + 1) folds each value into an accumulator that starts at 1, and negative inputs are refused because no factorial exists there.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Factorial of a Number with a Loop'.
questions.a: The accumulator begins at 1 because multiplying by 1 changes nothing, and the loop visits num values.

questions.q: Write the standard relation used for 'Factorial of a Number with a Loop', in plain ASCII form.

concepts.title: Sum of Even Numbers up to N

questions.q: Find the sum of all even numbers from 1 to 20 using the pairs formula.. Use the method 'Sum of Even Numbers up to N'. Work with: limit = 300. Carry the chain through step by step and give the final value of even_sum.
How many even numbers appear in the range 1 to 50? Use the method 'Sum of Even Numbers up to N'. Work with: limit = 240. Carry the chain through step by step and give the final value of even_sum.
Explain in your own words what 'Sum of Even Numbers up to N' refers to.
questions.a: A loop that tests num % 2 == 0 prints or adds only the even members of a sequence; up to a limit n there are n // 2 even numbers, and their total is half-count times half-count plus one.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Sum of Even Numbers up to N'.
questions.a: Every second number is even, so the count of evens below n is simply n // 2.

questions.q: Write the standard relation used for 'Sum of Even Numbers up to N', in plain ASCII form.

concepts.title: Loop Sum of a Cubed Sequence

questions.q: Using the method 'Loop Sum of a Cubed Sequence', work with: the fixed constants of the method. Carry the chain through step by step and give the final value of total.
Take the relation taught for 'Loop Sum of a Cubed Sequence' and work with: the fixed constants of the method. Carry the chain through step by step and give the final value of total.
Explain in your own words what 'Loop Sum of a Cubed Sequence' refers to.
questions.a: The sequence 1 + 1/8 + 1/27 + ... + 1/n cubed adds one reciprocal of a perfect cube per loop pass; each pass raises the counter to the power 3, divides 1 by it, and folds the term into the total.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Loop Sum of a Cubed Sequence'.
questions.a: Term k of the sequence equals 1 divided by k cubed, so the exponent operator builds every denominator.

questions.q: Write the standard relation used for 'Loop Sum of a Cubed Sequence', in plain ASCII form.
Explain in your own words what 'Elif Ladder for Grade Allocation' refers to.
questions.a: An if..elif..else chain tests grade boundaries from the top down: above 90 percent earns an A, 80 to 90 a B, 70 to 80 a C, 60 to 70 a D, and anything below lands in the final else block; the first true condition wins and the rest are skipped.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Elif Ladder for Grade Allocation'.
questions.a: Order matters in an elif ladder: testing the lowest band first would swallow every higher grade.

questions.q: Write the standard relation used for 'Elif Ladder for Grade Allocation', in plain ASCII form.
Explain in your own words what 'Break and Continue Statements' refers to.
questions.a: The break statement abandons the loop entirely and jumps to the first statement after it, while continue abandons only the current pass and returns to the loop's condition for the next pass.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Break and Continue Statements'.
questions.a: Break answers 'stop everything', continue answers 'skip this one', and mixing them up changes the output count.

questions.q: Write the standard relation used for 'Break and Continue Statements', in plain ASCII form.
questions.a: break -> exit loop; continue -> next iteration
